opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think time is one of the most underappreciated constraints. People often frame model development as being bottlenecked on compute, and compute obviously matters a lot. But even with all the compute you want, there's a sequential nature to the work that's hard to get around.

When you're training a large model, you can't really parallelize the whole thing. A big pretraining run takes months, and you're mostly locked into decisions you made before it started: the architecture, the data mix, the hyperparameters. So before that run, you need a lot of smaller experiments to de-risk those choices. You run small models, look at scaling trends, check whether an idea that helps at small scale still helps at larger scale. Each of those experiments takes time, and often the next experiment depends on what you learned from the last one. That chain of dependent experiments is basically your critical path.

So a lot of my thinking is about how to shorten that loop. How fast can a researcher go from having an idea to getting a trustworthy answer? That's partly infrastructure: making jobs launch reliably, making failures easy to debug, making sure people aren't stuck waiting on tooling. It's partly experimental design: choosing the smallest, cheapest experiment that actually answers the question. And it's partly prioritization, because you can only run so many things, so picking the right ones matters a lot.

Then there's the big run itself, where time is very costly. If something breaks, say a hardware failure, a loss spike, or a subtle bug, every day you spend diagnosing it is a day the whole cluster isn't doing useful work, and it pushes everything after it. So a lot of effort goes into reliability and monitoring, so you catch problems quickly and recover without losing much progress.

There's also a fixed cadence at the organizational level. You get a fairly small number of really big shots per year. That makes each one high stakes, and it means the research leading into it needs to be ready on time. You can have a great idea, but if it isn't validated when the run starts, it waits for the next generation.

So when I think about speeding things up, it's less "how do we get more GPUs" and more "how do we make every iteration faster, and how do we avoid wasting the serial time we can't get back."

r001.rationale: The candidate says each experiment often depends on what was learned from the previous one, creating a chain of dependent experiments that is hard to parallelize.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think time is actually one of the biggest constraints, and it's not always the one people think about first. People tend to focus on compute, or on data, or on the number of researchers you have. But a lot of what we do is fundamentally serial.

The way I'd put it is: training a big model takes a fixed amount of wall-clock time. You can't just throw more people at it and have it finish faster. Once you've committed to a run, you're waiting weeks or months for it to complete, and in the meantime you've got all these decisions you had to make up front, about the architecture, the data mix, the hyperparameters, and you don't get to see whether they were right until the end.

So a lot of the engineering is about de-risking those decisions ahead of time. You run a lot of smaller experiments, you try to build scaling laws so you can predict what the big run will do from what the small runs did. But every one of those experiments also takes time, and there's a limit to how many you can run in parallel before you're just bottlenecked on how many ideas you can actually think of and evaluate carefully.

And then there's the human side of it. The people who deeply understand the whole system, end to end, are pretty rare, and their time gets spread thin. If something goes wrong mid-run, say a loss spike, or some hardware failure that's subtly corrupting things, you need those people to diagnose it, and you're burning compute while they do. So it's not just that the run takes a long time, it's that the critical path runs through a small number of people's attention.

The way I think about it is that you have a certain number of "shots" per year at a frontier model. Maybe a handful. And every mistake that costs you a month is a meaningful fraction of your total iteration budget. That's really different from most software, where if you ship a bug you fix it the next day. Here the feedback loop is much slower, so you have to be much more deliberate up front, and you want to squeeze as much learning out of each run as you possibly can.

r001.rationale: The response says research is partly serial and that small experiments inform predictions for a large run, but it does not clearly state that designing the next experiment depends on understanding gained from earlier experiments.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between the time you spend doing the work and the time you spend waiting to learn whether the work was useful. You can have a lot of compute and a lot of people, but some parts of developing a model are sequential. You run an experiment, see what happens, and then decide what to try next. You can’t necessarily make those steps happen simultaneously by adding more resources.

So the bottleneck is often the length of that feedback loop. If an experiment takes a long time, you get fewer opportunities to discover that an assumption was wrong and change direction before you need to commit to a larger training run.

That makes fast, informative experiments really valuable. It also means you want to be thoughtful about which decisions actually need to wait for a result, and which work you can do in parallel. The goal is to learn enough, early enough, that you’re making the big decisions with useful evidence.

r001.rationale: The response says experiments produce results that inform what to try next, making parts of model development sequential and not fully parallelisable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of time as a constraint that interacts with almost everything else. You might have the compute to run a larger experiment, but if it takes six months, you get fewer opportunities to learn from the result and change course. So it’s not just how much computation you can do; it’s how many cycles of trying something, understanding what happened, and improving it you can fit in.

And those cycles have dependencies. Some experiments you can run in parallel, but others only become useful once you’ve seen the previous result. Adding more people or more machines doesn’t necessarily shorten that sequence.

That means a smaller experiment that gives you an answer quickly can sometimes be more valuable than a much larger one. The question is: what do we need to learn before committing to the next model, and how quickly can we get reliable evidence about it?

r001.rationale: The response says some experiments depend on seeing the previous result, and that added people or machines cannot necessarily shorten that sequence, clearly conveying why research cannot be fully parallelised.
